primary_claim: Implementing strategic attack selection (start/stop policies) for the red team in an agentic AI control evaluation (BashArena) substantially decreases blue-team safety relative to a fixed always-attack baseline, with the start policy driving nearly all of the effect and the stop policy having weak effects on already-selected attack datasets.

effect.metric: empirical safety (blue-team win rate) at fixed audit budget
effect.value: at 5% audit budget, top-1% selective attacker ~0.2 safety vs ~0.4 for no selection

contradicts_or_qualifies: Prior AI control evaluations that model attackers with a fixed or i.i.d. attack insertion rate may overstate safety and robustness against a truly adaptive, selective attacker
stated_future_work: Distinguishing whether the weak stop-policy result is because successful-before-caught windows are genuinely rare/narrow or because the learned stop policy fails to identify them
Evaluating attacker mechanisms of choosing when to prepare for an attack and when to de-escalate one
Testing whether patterns hold for a much stronger red-team stop-policy model
Allowing the blue team to adapt its monitor, protocol, or calibration once attack selection is in scope
limitations_stated: Only iterated to improve red-team attack selection and did not iterate on or re-optimize the blue team
Stop policy applied post-hoc after trajectories are recorded; in deployment the stop decision would feed back into the agent's future actions
Small-sample noise: with small cohorts individual trajectories can greatly affect RT success rate
Results primarily from BashArena, with only a small LinuxArena pilot for start-time selection
Unclear how large the safety gap is with stronger monitors, different task distributions, or longer trajectories
quote: At a 5% audit budget, the top-1% selective attacker faces roughly 0.2 safety versus roughly 0.4 for no selection.
